opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it was just accepting that we didn't know what the right answer was, and that this was okay. When we started TVM, there wasn't really a thing called a "deep learning compiler." People were writing hand-tuned kernels for each operator on each piece of hardware, and that clearly wasn't going to scale as models and hardware kept multiplying. So the problem was obvious, but the solution wasn't.

The way I approached it was to start from a concrete pain point instead of a grand design. We wanted to run models efficiently on more kinds of hardware, from GPUs to phones to new accelerators. So we built the smallest thing that could work end to end, got it running on real models, and then looked at where it broke. A lot of the early abstractions, like separating what you compute from how you schedule it, came from borrowing ideas from places like Halide and adapting them, not from inventing everything from scratch.

The second thing was being willing to throw things away. Some of our early designs turned out to be wrong, and we rewrote big parts of the system more than once. In research you can get attached to your first idea, but with something like a compiler, the field moves so fast that you have to keep iterating.

The third thing, which I think mattered most, was building it in the open with a community. I learned that from my earlier work on XGBoost. When you don't know the answer, having real users with real workloads tell you what's missing is incredibly valuable. Many of the most important directions in TVM came from people using it on hardware we didn't even have access to.

So I'd say: pick a real problem, build end to end early, stay humble about your abstractions, and let the community help you find the path. The uncertainty is actually what makes it exciting, because it means there's something genuinely new to discover.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I don't think I ever framed it as "there's no deep-learning compiler, so let's build one." It started much smaller than that. When we were working on MXNet, we kept running into the same wall: every time a new hardware target showed up, or someone wanted a new fused operator, somebody had to sit down and hand-write kernels. It was painfully repetitive, and the fast kernels only existed for a few vendors who could afford to pay engineers to do it. So the question wasn't really "should we build a compiler," it was "why are we writing the same thing over and over, and is there a way to not do that?"

That framing helped with the uncertainty, because the uncertainty was real. In 2016, 2017, the common wisdom was that you'd never beat cuDNN with generated code, and a lot of very smart people told me that. And they weren't wrong about the state of things at the time. What I leaned on was that the problem decomposed. Halide had already shown you could separate what you compute from how you schedule it for image processing. Deep-learning workloads looked like a big, somewhat different instance of the same thing. So I wasn't betting on one giant idea, I was betting that a few known ideas, put together in a new domain, would get you somewhere. That's a much easier bet to make.

The other thing is that I tried to make the early milestones very concrete and very humbling. The first goal wasn't "replace cuDNN." It was "can we get a conv2d on a Mali GPU to run at all, and then can we get it to not be embarrassing." Nobody else cared about Mali, so there was no baseline to lose to. Those edge targets, ARM phones, FPGAs, were where the pain was worst and the competition was thinnest, and every little win there taught us something that transferred back to the big targets.

And then I'd say the thing that mattered most was building it in the open from the start. When you're uncertain, the worst thing you can do is go into a cave for two years. We put TVM out early, when it was rough, and people from Amazon, from Huawei, from random grad students showed up and tried it on hardware we'd never seen. That feedback loop shrinks the uncertainty much faster than any amount of planning. A lot of what looks like foresight in retrospect was really just that we exposed ourselves to the problem space quickly and let it correct us.

So if I had to summarize: decompose the big scary thing into pieces you already half-understand, pick a corner where you can't be wrong in an embarrassing way, and open it up early so reality can push back on you. Then just keep going. The compiler part came later than people think. The habit of not giving up came first.

astra-6.text:
I think the way to approach that uncertainty is to make the next question concrete. You have this big goal—can we build a compiler that makes deep-learning models run efficiently across different hardware? But you don’t have to know the entire answer at the beginning. You can start with a small example, build something, measure it, and learn where your assumptions break.

I also wouldn’t frame it as starting from nothing. There were ideas from compilers and machine learning to build on. The uncertainty was how to bring those ideas together and which abstractions would work.

So the approach is iterative: have a direction, but be willing to change the design based on evidence. And make it possible for other people to contribute their workloads and hardware perspectives. That helps turn a problem you can’t fully anticipate into a set of concrete problems you can work through together.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the way to approach that uncertainty is to start with a concrete problem. We wanted to make it easier to run deep-learning models on different hardware, and we didn’t know in advance what the whole solution should look like. So you build something small, see where it works and where it breaks, and use that feedback to decide the next step.

There are also ideas you can draw on from compilers and systems, even when the particular problem is new. You form a hypothesis, build a prototype, and test it. That doesn’t remove the uncertainty, but it makes it manageable. You don’t have to know every step at the beginning; you need a useful direction and a way to keep learning.
